newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan yawns at star copper trader"s day in court.
newsitem.headline: Japan yawns at star copper trader"s day in court.

text.p: Former Sumitomo copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka had his day in court on Monday, but as far as the Japanese media were concerned the spectacular $2.6 billion scandal could have been an ordinary shoplifting case.

Japanese television stations, which fill the air with helicopters to cover politicians" arrests and last year paid students $100 each to queue for spectators seats at the Tokyo subway gassing trial, gave a yawn to the fallen star of copper trading.
"How can we explain and analyse something we don"t understand," quipped a Japanese journalist after hearing prosecutors detail Hamanaka"s complex web of international copper derivatives trades.

Japanese newspapers made no mention of the case in their morning editions on trial day and Tokyo"s news agencies held back on the bulletin treatment they customarily give to the mundane remarks of cabinet ministers.
Court authorities apparently agreed that the trial was not going to be a "hot ticket".

It took place in courtroom number 522 at Tokyo District Court, a small, sterile-looking white room with wooden furniture, the same size as chambers nearby in which several Japanese men were on trial for robbery and narcotics charges and a Chinese woman faced illegal immigration charges.
Hamanaka pleaded guilty to fraud and forgery at the start of Monday"s hearing, and could face up to 15 years in prison.

His trial, closely watched abroad for any clues it may shed on whether there was any attempt to manipulate world copper prices, was a far cry from the opening session of the subway gassing murder trial of guru Shoko Asahara.

On that April day last year, police sealed off the six-lane street in front of the court building, and thousands gathered for a lottery to decide who would be allowed sit in the 48 public spectator seats.
